messages.content: Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

Six months in, here's the piece of our mentorship program I got wrong.

Version one was a spreadsheet. Junior in column A, senior in column B, meet weekly. By week four, three pairs had quietly stopped meeting and nobody mentioned it. The seniors had decided they were now accountable for someone else's performance review. The juniors were turning up to a blank hour, unsure what they were even allowed to ask for.

What fixed it was shrinking the thing. Each pair now names one outcome for the quarter — learn the deploy pipeline cold, run a design review end to end, write a doc that survives the staff engineers. Write it down. Look at it in twelve weeks. Finish early and you either pick something new or you stop. Stopping is a fine answer.

The reporting went too. No dashboard, no percent complete. One number: pairs still meeting in month three. Seven of nine today.

Two things caught me off guard. Our best mentors weren't the most senior people, they were engineers roughly two years ahead, still close enough to remember which parts had been confusing. And the mentors got more from it than the mentees. Three of them said it was the first time in years anybody had asked them to explain out loud why they work the way they do.

If you're starting one: five pairs, not twenty. Hand each pair a question to answer rather than a relationship to keep alive. Check in at week six, and let the ones that aren't working die there.

output:
Half a year in, and the part of our mentorship program I most want back is the beginning.

The first version was a spreadsheet. Junior on the left, senior on the right, meet every week. By the end of month one, three pairs had gone silent and nobody said anything about it. The seniors had concluded they were on the hook for another person's review cycle. The juniors showed up to an empty hour with no idea what they were permitted to ask.

The fix was making it smaller. Every pair now picks one thing to get done in a quarter: know the deploy pipeline inside out, lead a design review start to finish, write a doc the staff engineers don't tear apart. Put it in writing. Revisit it at week twelve. If you get there early, choose another one or call it done. Calling it done is allowed.

I dropped the reporting too. No dashboard, no completion bar. Just one figure: how many pairs are still meeting in month three. Right now that's seven out of nine.

Two surprises. The strongest mentors weren't the most senior engineers. They were people about two years further along, close enough to still remember what had tripped them up. And the mentors got more out of it than the mentees did. Three told me it had been years since anyone asked them to say out loud why they work the way they do.

Advice if you're setting one up: start with five pairs, not twenty. Give each pair a question to chase instead of a relationship to sustain. Check in at week six, and let the pairs that aren't working end there.
